clue.text: Do exercises in school

blocks.note: first meaning: to work out, practise for fitness
second meaning: as a verb, to instruct or coach someone

explanation.surface: A PE teacher telling pupils to work out during lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' looks like a place to exercise, but here it is a verb meaning to teach.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both practising physically for a sport and instructing someone in a skill.

clue.text: High flier up for trial?

blocks.note: surface reading: an ambitious high achiever facing a court case
setter's reading: someone who flies aircraft up in the sky to try them out

explanation.walkthrough: 'High flier' suggests a successful career person and 'trial' a court, but both are literal: an aviator and a test.
explanation.definitionFit: This person's job is flying new or modified aircraft to assess their performance and safety.

clue.text: Drop unresolved argument with side with a greater ego, possibly

indicators.note: possibly means the letters might be arranged some other way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Abandon a row with the more egotistical faction, maybe.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means both parties accept that they hold different views and stop arguing.

clue.text: Serviette, sort mostly used after game

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
what is used after something follows it, so this part goes second

blocks.note: nap is a card game
a sort is a kind

explanation.surface: A table napkin of the usual type is used once a match is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Nap, short for Napoleon, is an old card game where players bid on tricks.
explanation.definitionFit: A serviette is the British word for a cloth or paper square used at meals to wipe the mouth.

clue.text: Perform with copper and doctor, to a degree, in a sort of play

blocks.note: to do is to perform
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
DR is the abbreviation for doctor
taken as written
MA, a Master of Arts, is a university degree

explanation.surface: Someone is acting alongside a policeman and a doctor in a fairly standard drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to a degree' reads as 'somewhat', but it supplies A plus a degree; copper is the metal, not the policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: A docudrama is a dramatised presentation of real events, one particular genre of play or film.

clue.text: Put off, in crude terms

indicators.note: in means the letters are found inside the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of crude and the start of terms

explanation.surface: Someone was repelled by rough, blunt language.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter is to discourage someone from acting, which is what putting them off means.

clue.text: Inexpensive, flag of inferior quality

blocks.note: something inexpensive is cheap
a jack is a small flag flown on a ship, as in Union Jack

explanation.surface: A budget banner that is shoddily made.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapjack as an adjective describes goods that are shoddy and of low worth.

clue.text: Drawings of Mardi Gras, not right somehow

indicators.note: not right means the letter standing for right is left out
somehow means in some unknown way, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sketches of the carnival that are somehow off.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one of the two Rs from Mardi Gras before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Diagrams are simplified line drawings that show how something is laid out or works.

clue.text: Very little indeed of what returning US astronauts may expect?

definitions.text: what returning US astronauts may expect

blocks.note: first meaning: a tiny amount compared with what is needed

blocks.clueFragment: what returning US astronauts may expect
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: American space capsules came back by splashing down at sea

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading: Apollo crews fell from the sky into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a quantity so small that it makes no real difference.

clue.text: Earmark a tax to be raised

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word means reading it from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a toll is a levy for using a road or bridge

explanation.surface: Setting aside a levy that is going to be increased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' sounds like a tax increase, but it turns the word upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to assign or set aside for a purpose, just as earmarking does.

clue.text: Use the least useful thing available, and fix the lot!

definitions.text: Use the least useful thing available

blocks.note: a fix and a scrape are both awkward predicaments
taken as written
a barrel can mean a large quantity, a lot

explanation.surface: Someone grabs any old rubbish to hand and patches up everything with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fix' looks like a verb for repairing, but it is the noun meaning a tight spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means resorting to the poorest remaining resources because nothing better is left.

clue.text: Earliest PM

blocks.note: first meaning: first in time or rank
second meaning: a prime minister, as the head of government

explanation.surface: Seems to ask who was the first prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means first or foremost, and the noun is a common title for a prime minister.

clue.text: Appear in disguise close to ancient balustrade

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the word before it is rearranged
the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the last letter of ancient

explanation.surface: Someone shows up in costume beside an old stone balustrade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' reads as 'near' but means the end letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A parapet is a low protective wall or railing along a roof, bridge or balcony edge.

clue.text: Swag in sack

blocks.note: first meaning: stolen goods, a burglar's haul
second meaning: as a verb, to plunder a captured town

explanation.surface: A burglar's haul stuffed in a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sack' looks like the bag holding the swag, but it is the verb for pillaging.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is plunder taken by thieves, and the verb means to pillage a place.

clue.text: Saying there's doubtful merit talking with skinhead

indicators.note: something doubtful is uncertain and unsettled, so the following letters are not in a fixed order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A proverb suggesting there's little value in chatting with a skinhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saying' looks like part of the sentence's verb, but it is a noun meaning proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known proverb, said when two people independently have the same idea.

clue.text: Note amateur runs ahead of champion in track event

indicators.note: in a down clue, being ahead of something means sitting above it, so that part comes first

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
lay means non-professional
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
an ace is an expert or champion

explanation.surface: A note says an amateur athlete leads the champion on the track.
explanation.definitionFit: A relay race is a team running event in which each runner hands a baton to the next.

clue.text: Trivia is what one may get in the pub

definitions.text: what one may get in the pub

blocks.note: first meaning: matters of little importance

blocks.clueFragment: what one may get in the pub
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: a modest half-pint ordered at the bar

explanation.surface: Seems to talk about a pub quiz and what you might win in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trivia' suggests a pub quiz, but it means unimportant things.
explanation.definitionFit: Small beer was originally weak beer, so the phrase came to mean things of no consequence.

clue.text: Shallow type involved in leak

indicators.note: something involved in another is wrapped up within it, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: to seep is to leak slowly
a type is a kind

explanation.surface: A superficial sort of person caught up in a press leak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type' tempts as a description of a person, but it is just a synonym for sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Something skin-deep goes no further than the surface, like beauty in the proverb.

clue.text: See 13
Bird spotted in Leatherhead

indicators.note: something spotted in a place is seen inside it, so the answer sits within the next word

blocks.note: letters five to eight of the town's name

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher reports a sighting in Leatherhead, a town in Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless South American bird, related to the ostrich.

clue.text: Urge small number to have good warming drink

blocks.note: to egg on is to urge
No. is the short form of number
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Persuading a few people to have a nice hot drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small number' reads as 'a few', but it means the short form of the word number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a rich drink of eggs, milk and often spirits, traditionally served warm in winter.

clue.text: Little Bernard has line in flattery

indicators.note: one thing placed in another goes inside it, so the single letter is put within the name

blocks.note: Barney is a pet form of the name Bernard
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A young boy called Bernard has a sweet-talking line to use.
explanation.walkthrough: BARNEY takes L after its first letter. Blarney is named after the Irish castle stone said to give the gift of the gab.
explanation.definitionFit: Blarney is smooth, charming talk meant to flatter or persuade.

clue.text: Clubs in English city making a collection

indicators.note: in places one thing within the other

blocks.note: Bath is a spa city in Somerset
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Clubs in an English city forming a group or league.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes between the T and H of BATH.
explanation.definitionFit: A batch is a quantity of things grouped or produced together, a set.

clue.text: Cat shown in newspaper next to pretty girl

blocks.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
doll is slang for an attractive young woman

explanation.surface: A cat photo printed in the paper beside a pin-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ragdoll is a breed of large, docile domestic cat that goes limp when picked up.

clue.text: Poet may show anger about ending in limerick

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept
about means going around, so the anger word surrounds the single letter

blocks.note: to rile is to anger
the last letter of limerick

explanation.surface: A poet might get cross about how a limerick ends.
explanation.walkthrough: K goes between the L and E of RILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian lyric poet, author of the Duino Elegies.

clue.text: Ignored an untidy bleeder in resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, meaning to sort again, so the preceding letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone overlooked a scruffy rotter at a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'untidy' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the letters; 'resort' split as re-sort does the work. Bleeder is British slang for a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn a blind eye is the idiom for deliberately pretending not to notice something.

clue.text: Item on list, part of a shoe

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another follows it, so the first word comes second

blocks.note: a ship that lists heels over to one side
an item is a single piece

explanation.surface: A shopping list with a shoe component on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'list' looks like a written list, but it is the nautical lean.
explanation.definitionFit: A heelpiece is the part of a shoe forming or covering the heel.

clue.text: Person beyond saving, individual imprisoned by King George

indicators.note: something imprisoned is held within walls, so one piece is shut inside the other

blocks.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is King George's royal cipher
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: A doomed prisoner held in the dungeons of King George.
explanation.walkthrough: A monarch's cipher is the initial plus R for Rex or Regina, as seen on British postboxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is informal for someone who is dead or certain to die or fail.
